body: Whatever they have just mopped the supermarket floor with is the same thing a hospital used, and on a Tuesday in March a woman buying washing powder is standing in the aisle with a box in her hand, four years away from that corridor and also entirely inside it. It lasts perhaps forty seconds. Then she puts the box in the trolley, remembers she needs bin bags, and finishes the shop. She drives home. She puts the kettle on. Nobody who walked past her noticed a single thing.

Ask the people who know her and they will tell you she is doing well, and they will be right. She has work she likes. She sleeps most nights now. By every ordinary measure she is past it — and she is not over it, and both of those are true at once.
The word people reach for is over. Are you over it. She is not over it yet. He should be over it by now. It is such an ordinary word that nobody stops to look at the picture inside it.

The picture is a hurdle. Something stands in the track; you approach it, you clear it, and the ground beyond is the same flat ground as before, with the obstacle behind you and no longer any of your business. That metaphor is wrong for almost everything serious, and it does damage in both directions at once. The person carrying the thing hears that they are late — that there was an hour by which the hurdle ought to have been cleared, and that being unfinished is now a second problem sitting on the first. Everybody else is handed a schedule to measure them against, and with it a quiet licence to be impatient when it is not kept.
This band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air. One was built for the hours between midnight and morning, and named by people who know what goes on in them.

Beyond is a different word doing a different job, and it was chosen deliberately. It says a distance has been covered and says nothing whatever about the ground behind you having changed, which is the more expensive thing to put on a station, because it promises less. A frequency could have been called Healed. That would be a better name for getting attention and a worse one for telling the truth. Beyond means you have travelled. It does not mean the ground behind you has changed.

Language of that shape has become rare, because most of what gets said about recovery is built like a story, and stories want an ending. The testimony arc wants a before and an after with a clean line between them. The clinical version wants stages, and stages want an order and a final one. Neither is dishonest on purpose; both are simply under pressure to arrive somewhere, because an account that does not arrive is hard to tell in the time available. The person actually carrying it learns the shape they are supposed to be and starts performing it, which is the one thing guaranteed to stop them getting any further along.

So there is no healing hour on this dial. There is no programme that opens with a difficulty and closes, forty minutes later, with the difficulty resolved and a bed of strings underneath it. The stations run continuously on numbers that do not move; a station playing at eleven is still playing at four, and nothing on it is scheduled to conclude. That is not an absence of care. It is what care looks like once it has stopped trying to also be a narrative.
Which is the whole difference between something that keeps you company and something that keeps you to a timetable.

Be fair to the alternative first. A person in the worst part of it will often make themselves a playlist, and it can be a genuinely good thing to do — twenty songs that say the thing they cannot say, available at two in the morning without asking anybody. But a playlist made in grief is made by the griever, and can only contain what they were able to think of on the day they made it. It becomes a room with the curtains drawn, which is sometimes exactly the room required, and it has no window. Play it for six months and it is still handing back the person who assembled it, at the worst hour of their worst year, with terrible accuracy.
Beyond is a distance. Over is a deadline.

It is ten past three and a man is standing in his kitchen in a dressing gown waiting for the kettle, because lying still had stopped being restful an hour ago. He has not turned the radio on; it has been on since yesterday, because he never turns it off, and something slow is playing that he does not recognise and will not remember. He does not pray. He watches the security light on next door’s shed come on for a cat and go off again. At twenty to four he goes back up and sleeps until seven. That is the whole of it. There is no moment in it, it happens perhaps three nights in ten, and it is a large part of why he is upright at his daughter’s wedding in June.

Nothing in that kitchen had been arranged for him, and nothing in it asked how he was getting on. That is the mechanism. Company that makes no enquiries is the only kind some people can bear at that hour.

It is only honest to say what this does not do. A radio station does not heal anybody. It will not shorten anything by a single week. Some nights it will make matters worse — a song will arrive with her voice in it, or his, and the room will open up when you had it deliberately shut. And there are people who will carry what they carry to the end of their lives and not be restored in this one. That is in the Bible too, in more places than are comfortable, and it is not tidied up there either.

But notice what a station is not doing to you while it fails to fix you. It is not measuring you. It holds no view on how long this has taken and no stage you ought to have reached by now. It simply keeps playing, on the good nights and the bad ones alike, and it will still be there next March at the same number. Very little else makes that offer without also making a demand.

So beyond is the honest word, and this band uses it on purpose. It does not claim the thing is gone, or smaller, or that a Tuesday in a supermarket cannot still take forty seconds off you four years later. It claims a distance has been travelled and that more country has opened up on the far side — that the map is no longer organised entirely around one place. That is worth naming plainly, because the alternative teaches people to perform a recovery they have not been given.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

The dial carries four kinds of programming, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of the band — worship, hymns, gospel, country, rap, ambient and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, playable in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards — 40 across 29 languages. Every station holds one frequency permanently, so once you have found a number you can go back to it in the dark.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 314.40 — Midnight Praise. It is Nova Inspire’s contemplative catalogue, Celtic and European ambient worship, built for the long night, the overnight watch and the people who are simply still awake. It is slow, largely wordless, and it does not raise its voice at you. That last part is the reason to name this frequency rather than another in an article about something that is not over. A lyric makes a claim, and at three in the morning a claim is more than you can take a position on; being asked to agree or disagree is its own small exhaustion. Midnight Praise mostly does not make claims. It occupies the room without filling it, and asks you for nothing back.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you want it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for at four in the morning — which is how the next station for those hours gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an offer. Do not assess it and do not give it a fair trial; those are words for making a decision, and this is not a decision. Put HM 314.40 on tonight before you go up, and then leave it alone. Let it be playing if you come down at three, and let it be playing if you do not. You are not required to be over anything by the morning. You are only required to be further along than you were, and if you are reading this at all, you already are.
